lines: Here's a strange little experiment that actually happened.
The very same recommendation went out twice, written at two wildly different lengths, and only one of those two versions ever got read all the way through.
The room with five minutes to spare could act on the short one. It genuinely could not act on the long one, no matter how sound the reasoning inside it turned out to be.
So why did the identical recommendation land so differently in that very same room.
What changed, if the underlying decision itself never did.
answer: Not the decision, and not the facts sitting behind it either.
The document's own length and shape decided whether that room could actually act on it in the time it genuinely had.

lines: Here are the very same three tiers from the last topic, restated once again.
Not in the compute, storage and pipeline terms that originally built them.
Instead, in dollars, and in the real risk of a wrong number ever reaching a plant manager, which is what a decision maker actually weighs.
Of everything that makes the fast tier so expensive, one single factor drives nearly all of that gap.
How often the whole thing recomputes itself.
That one factor gets named explicitly here, rather than buried inside a list of five equally weighted factors nobody can actually act on.
The medium tier is not the fastest option on offer, and that turns out to be exactly the argument for recommending it.
That argument gets stated and defended in terms a non engineer actually weighs, cost and risk, rather than assumed as some engineering instinct nobody ever has to explain out loud.
There's a real, well documented practice worth borrowing here.
Write the conclusion first, in one single page, for the room that only has five minutes to spare.
Then write a separate, far longer document for the review that actually has to check the reasoning behind it.
The one page version carries the recommendation itself, its cost, and that one dominant lever.
The deep dive carries the full tier comparison, every single non goal, and the error budget math behind it.
Same decision, two separate documents, and neither one lying by omission to its own audience.
Pulling this together now.
The same decision, restated in business terms, its one dominant lever named plainly, a boring choice defended on purpose, and a one page summary paired with the deep dive sitting right behind it.
None of those four pieces is actually optional.
A stakeholder reads only the one page summary's bottom line, and approves the fast tier, purely because faster sounds strictly better.
So what's genuinely missing from that one page summary itself, that would have actually stopped this.
answer: Not more length added to the page.
That one page summary itself still has to state its own recommended tier and name its own dominant cost lever, or a reader who stops right at the first number ends up approving the wrong one.
